summary: B is substantially closer to the frozen contract: it exposes the exact Upload signature, reuses multipartbody.NewFile, preserves FilesOption, validates inputs, and verifies multipart encoding and retries. A introduces explicitly forbidden APIs and broad machinery.
reasons: B implements the required Upload(ctx, fileName, content, opts ...FilesOption) signature; A substitutes a new AddFileOption API.
B directly reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile. A unnecessarily extends the helper with NewFileWithFields to support association fields that the contract explicitly forbids.
A adds multiple public association options and duplicate query/request-option machinery, violating scope and changing the required option model.

A globally buffers every non-replayable RawClient body and silently ignores io.ReadAll failures after potentially consuming part of the body, creating corrupt-request and error-semantics risks. B limits its lower-level retry change to seekable readers used by the reported Files.Add case and tests offsets and non-replayable behavior explicitly before leaving it unchanged. B's Upload itself remains replayable through the established in-memory helper; its retry test does not depend on the seekable-body change, which is good separation of the two reported behaviors.
risks_a: Upload bypasses FilesService.Add instead of routing through it.
It violates the exact API contract with AddFileOption and adds expressly forbidden association fields.

makeBodyReplayable can consume part of a failing reader, suppress the error, and then send a truncated remainder without retries. It also broadens in-memory buffering to all RawClient reader bodies, beyond the approved upload path. The multipart helper extension and sorted-field machinery are unnecessary repository churn, and tests omit source-reader failures.
risks_b: Upload duplicates Add's request, decoding, and error logic instead of calling Add as explicitly required, creating future drift risk.
The seekable RawClient wrapper broadly changes body-closing ownership and transfer semantics, although it is targeted at the reported existing Add failure and is documented and tested.
Tests do not cover propagation of a source-reader error, despite the contract explicitly requiring that verification.
